Analysis:

Alert triggered for CTM-Privileged SA Account Scanning Activity from Non-Approved Scanner IP.

Log Source Time: Sep 15, 2026, 1:06:31 AM

Event Name: Success Audit: An account was successfully logged on
Low Level Category: User Login Success

Observed Source IP: 10.69.219.26 towards destination IP: 10.69.219.74

Both Ip's are internal only.

Source Host: INGTDCBRKWA05
Destination Host: CDCINTDEVDC04
Account: sa01.intappdevnxau
Authentication Package: NTLM
Logon Type: 3 (Network Logon)

As checked alert details, multiple 4624 Successful Logon events were observed for account INTAPPSROOTDEV\sa01.intappdevnxau.

Observed details:
Logon Type : 3 (Network)
Authentication Package : NTLM
Workstation Name : INGTDCBRKWA05
Source Network Address : 10.69.219.26
Destination Host : CDCINTDEVDC04
Windows_DC_hostname (custom): cdcintdevdc04.Intappsrootdev.net

The alert was triggered because a privileged service account sa01.intappdevnxau successfully authenticated over the network from 10.69.219.26 to 10.69.219.74, which matched the rule CTM-Privileged SA Account Scanning Activity from Non-Approved Scanner IP.

As checked payload, the logon was successful and generated Windows Event ID:
4624 - An account was successfully logged on

The authentication occurred using: NTLM V2
Logon Type 3 (Network Logon)
which is commonly observed for service-to-service communication, scheduled tasks, application connectivity, remote authentication, or automated processes.

As checked source IP logs for the last 7 days, normal server activity was observed, including:
Successful logon events, Process creation events, SplunkForwarder activity, WinCollect activity, Firewall permit events,
Kerberos ticket activity, Network share access activity

No evidence of failed login attempts, privilege escalation, malware execution, suspicious processes, lateral movement, or unauthorized access was observed during the investigation.

The observed activity appears consistent with legitimate service account authentication from host INGTDCBRKWA05 to the destination system.

Other than this, nothing suspicious observed.

For further investigation checking with CDC team.

Hence, closing this case as false positive.

Analysis:

Alert triggered for suspicious download activity detected by Zscaler NSS and matched the use case CTM-New threat detected as per Zscaler threat category.

Source IP: 192.168.1.9

File Name: acrordrdcx64upd2600221901_incr.msi

User Agent: Microsoft BITS/7.8
Action: Allowed
URL Category: TCS_Allowed_URLs
SSL Inspection: Enabled
Risk Score: 50
Threat Name: suspicious

Malware Class: None

The event indicates that the user system downloaded an Adobe Acrobat Reader update package (MSI installer) from the official Adobe download domain ardownload3.adobe.com.

The file name pattern "acrordrdcx64upd2600221901_incr.msi" is consistent with legitimate Adobe Acrobat Reader incremental update packages. The download was performed using Microsoft BITS (Background Intelligent Transfer Service), which is commonly used by software update mechanisms.

The destination domain belongs to Adobe's official software distribution infrastructure and is categorized under TCS_Allowed_URLs. 
No malware signature, sandbox detection, or malicious classification was observed in the event.

Although the Threat Name is marked as "suspicious" and Risk Score is 50, the file was allowed by policy and no malware detection verdict was generated. 
The file was marked as UNSCANNABLE, meaning Zscaler could not fully inspect the file content, but there is no indication of malicious activity based on the available logs.

No evidence of malware execution, command-and-control communication, unauthorized downloads, credential theft, or compromise was observed.
The activity is consistent with a legitimate Adobe Acrobat Reader software update download from an approved vendor source.

No malicious activity was identified.
Hence closing this case as False Positive.

The email appears to be a fake Geek Squad subscription invoice and callback-based tech-support scam.

The subject, “Daniel Jennifer Greer,” is unrelated to the alleged purchase or renewal.
The sender uses an unrelated personal Outlook address while impersonating Geek Squad.
The message claims that order 737 was received and prominently displays the help-desk number +1 864 856 3745.
The attached PDF claims that a Geek Squad Security Plan subscription was renewed for two years.
The PDF lists a charge of $306.73 and marks the order as confirmed.
The invoice claims that the subscription will automatically renew every two years unless disabled.
The recipient is instructed to call +1 864 856 3745 within a limited time for a “full reversal” if the payment was not approved.
The repeated phone number, unexpected charge, unrelated sender address, unusual subject, and urgency around reversing the payment are typical indicators of a refund or tech-support scam.

Attack Objective: Callback phishing and social engineering
 Classification: Phishing / Tech-Support Scam / Fake Invoice

CustomFields.investigationanalysis:
Analysis:

The offense "CTM-Cisco ISE Brute Force Authentication Attempt Detection" was triggered due to a high volume of Cisco ISE RADIUS authentication failures observed from source IP 10.249.147.10 and 10.249.147.13 toward Cisco ISE server 10.249.250.246 over port 1812 (RADIUS).

Investigation revealed multiple authentication failure events originating from internal source IP, directed towards the internal Cisco ISE server 10.249.250.246 over RADIUS port 1812.

Observed Details:
Username/MAC Address: B4-45-06-70-93-97
Authentication Method: MAB (MAC Authentication Bypass)
Event Category: General Authentication Failed
Event Outcome: Authentication Failed

Analysis of the logs confirmed repeated FAILED_ATTEMPT events associated with the same MAC address.
The authentication requests were generated through the MAB process and forwarded by internal network devices/switches to Cisco ISE as part of the organization's Network Access Control (NAC) mechanism. The correlation rule was triggered due to the high volume of authentication failures observed for a single endpoint identifier.

Further review indicates that the activity is associated with a device using MAC address B0-7B-25-6E-BD-FA repeatedly attempting network authentication but failing Cisco ISE authorization.
The logs indicate the authentication method as MAB (cisco-av-pair=method=mab), with the username corresponding to the device MAC address rather than a user account.
This behavior is consistent with an unregistered, unauthorized, or misconfigured endpoint and is not indicative of a password-based brute-force attack.

No evidence of successful authentication, account compromise, privilege escalation, lateral movement, malicious scanning, or unauthorized network access was identified during the investigation. Additionally, the authentication failures were limited to MAB-based endpoint validation and did not involve interactive user credential login attempts.

Based on the available evidence, the observed activity is assessed as a legitimate network access control event caused by repeated MAB authentication failures. Therefore, this offense is determined to be a False Positive

Analysis:
Alert triggered for Reported ANTISPAM/Phishing Email - Email Investigation
As checked sender ID seen as shs.woodbridge@outlook.com
sub line : DEAR FRIENDS & FAMILY JOIN ME FOR A JOYFUL GATHERING FROM SPRINGHAILL SUITES..!!!

The email uses an event invitation theme and impersonates Evite while directing users to a non-Evite domain. The content references social media, privacy pages, and legitimate Evite branding, but the actual invitation URLs point to unrelated infrastructure.

The email impersonates Evite and encourages recipients to open an invitation or RSVP. However, the primary call-to-action links redirect to fruitsplace[.]guru rather than an official Evite domain, indicating suspicious redirection behaviour.

When accessed the link present in mail body:
hxxps[:]//guest[.]fruitsplace.guru/index.php
When the embedded URL was accessed, the sandbox observed the download and execution of ScreenConnect.ClientSetup.exe. The file installed ConnectWise Screen Connect Organization, a remote access tool
The email uses brand impersonation and a fake invitation lure to deliver a remote access tool (RAT) disguised as an event invitation.

Verdict:
Phishing
Malware Delivery

Sub-Category: Brand Impersonation / Invitation Lure
action taken : sender id blocking and email deletion

investigationanalysis:
Analysis:
Alert triggered for Reported ANTISPAM/Phishing Email - Email Investigation
As checked sender ID seen as shs.woodbridge@outlook.com
sub line : DEAR FRIENDS & FAMILY JOIN ME FOR A JOYFUL GATHERING FROM SPRINGHAILL SUITES..!!!

The email uses an event invitation theme and impersonates Evite while directing users to a non-Evite domain. The content references social media, privacy pages, and legitimate Evite branding, but the actual invitation URLs point to unrelated infrastructure.

The email impersonates Evite and encourages recipients to open an invitation or RSVP. However, the primary call-to-action links redirect to fruitsplace[.]guru rather than an official Evite domain, indicating suspicious redirection behaviour.

When accessed the link present in mail body:
hxxps[:]//guest[.]fruitsplace.guru/index.php
When the embedded URL was accessed, the sandbox observed the download and execution of ScreenConnect.ClientSetup.exe. The file installed ConnectWise Screen Connect Organization, a remote access tool
The email uses brand impersonation and a fake invitation lure to deliver a remote access tool (RAT) disguised as an event invitation.

Verdict:
Phishing
Malware Delivery

Sub-Category: Brand Impersonation / Invitation Lure
action taken : sender id blocking and email deletion
closing as TP with no impact

CustomFields.investigationanalysis:
Analysis:
Alert triggered for Cisco ISE Brute Force Authentication Attempt Detection
Offence source observed as Username - B4-45-06-70-A9-67
Where source IP observed as 10.249.147.10 & dest IP observed as 10.249.250.246 
Both the source IP and destination IP are internal IPs only

As checked alerted events, observed multiple " FAILED_ATTEMPT " events around alert time.
Where Device Name observed as - TCS-KOL-INFOSPACE-CITI-6H1-ASW1

This event appears to be a failed Cisco ISE MAB authentication attempt for endpoint MAC address B4:45:06:70:A9:67 on switch TCS-KOL-INFOSPACE-CITI-6H1-ASW1 (Gi1/0/11). 
The authentication was denied by Cisco ISE during RADIUS processing.
Failure likely means the device is not recognized or not allowed in ISE.

Further we have checked user’s logs, No success events observed.
Alert triggered when at least 200 events are seen with the same Username in 1 minutes
No other suspicious activities observed from logs.
Hence closing this case as false positive.

As checked sender ID seen as ivangrantp6ja2gb2@outlook.com
Recipient seen as sanjay.vaidya@tcs.com
subject line : John Dean

no links observed
1 pdf attachment . Attachment contains a fake Geek Squad renewal invoice

The attached PDF claims that a Geek Squad Tech Support Ultimate subscription has been renewed successfully and that a payment of $234.99 has been processed through auto-renewal. The document provides a support number for cancellation or billing concerns and creates urgency around an unauthorized charge scenario. The use of a fake renewal confirmation, invoice details, and callback number is consistent with a Geek Squad-themed callback phishing campaign.

Verdict : Fraudulent Invoice Scam
Action : Sender ID Blocking
Hence closing as TP with no impact

CustomFields.investigationanalysis:
Analysis:

Alert triggered for a suspicious web request against Bizreview.ultimatix.net.
The event was generated by F5 ASM WAF and matched the violation "HTTP Compliance Failure - Host header contains IP address".

Source IP: 34.26.156.133
Destination IP: 10.40.50.220
Request Method: GET
Request URI:
/api/download?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/

Attack Type: HTTP Parser Attack / SSRF Attempt
Action: Blocked
User Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Ubuntu; Linux x86_64) Chrome/131.0.5432.32 Safari/537.36; compatible; Claude-User/1.0
Location: United States

The event indicates an attempt to exploit a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability by forcing the application to fetch data from the AWS Instance Metadata Service.
The payload targeted:
http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/

which is a well-known AWS metadata endpoint used to retrieve IAM role credentials and temporary access tokens assigned to cloud instances.
The request also contained suspicious metadata-related headers:
Metadata: true
Metadata-Flavor: Google

and used an IP address in the Host header, resulting in an HTTP protocol compliance violation.
The activity originated from an external source and targeted a public-facing application protected by F5 ASM WAF. 
The request was successfully blocked before reaching the backend application.

No evidence of successful metadata access, credential disclosure, unauthorized cloud access, privilege escalation, or compromise was observed in the available logs.
The observed behavior is consistent with automated vulnerability scanning, reconnaissance activity, or active SSRF exploitation attempts targeting cloud-hosted applications.

This alert is triggered due to an SSRF pattern attempting to access cloud instance metadata credentials and an HTTP compliance violation detected by F5 ASM WAF.
The activity is malicious in nature; however, the attack was successfully prevented by existing security controls.

Hence closing this case as True Positive.

CustomFields.investigationanalysis:
Analysis:
An alert was triggered for the file “com.apple.WebKit.Networking” under the Tactic & Technique “Custom Intelligence via Indicator of Compromise” on host “02HW062525”.
No action taken by CS.
No details of hash found in VT.
File name: com.apple.WebKit.Networking
File path: /System/Volumes/Preboot/Cryptexes/Incoming/OS/System/Library/Frameworks/WebKit.framework/Versions/A/XPCServices/com.apple.WebKit.Networking.xpc/Contents/MacOS/com.apple.WebKit.Networking
Command line: /System/Library/Frameworks/WebKit.framework/Versions/A/XPCServices/com.apple.WebKit.Networking.xpc/Contents/MacOS/com.apple.WebKit.Networking
Triggering indicator observed is the IP “3.85.177.52” (Amazon Data Services Northern Virginia) which matched the critical custom IOC.
launchd > com.apple.WebKit.Networking were the observed parent process, which is legitimate
No registry and process operations. In network operations, multiple amazon, akamai and other IPs observed.
“com.apple.WebKit.Networking” is a macOS/iOS system process that belongs to WebKit, Apple’s web rendering engine used by Safari and many apps that display web content. In short, this process handles the networking tasks for web content in  MacOS.
CrowdStrike generated the alert because the Apple WebKit networking process (com.apple.WebKit.Networking) initiated or was associated with communication to IP “3.85.177.52”, which matched a custom IOC marked as Critical.
Further checked timeline logs, there was no evidence of “com.apple.WebKit.Networking” communicating with IOC IP “3.85.177.52”
Team already Further checked with L3, initially this IP was associated with “CobaltStrike”, thus it was marked as critical IOC. Later, it will be removed from the critical IOC list.
Hence, closing this alert as false positive.

CustomFields.triageexplanation:
Excel was launched to open a spreadsheet directly from an Outlook attachment cache location (`…\AppData\Local\Microsoft\Olk\Attachments\…\TCS Commercial Summary 21Jul2026_NM_WIP.xlsx`). As the file was opened, Falcon’s cloud-based machine learning and document/macro inspection logic evaluated the workbook’s embedded macro content and metadata (for example, macro identifiers and display names) rather than relying on a user-visible “detection description.” Based on what was found inside the document, Charlotte AI triaged this activity as a confirmed detection associated with the Laroux macro family.

This was triaged as a true positive because the workbook’s macro characteristics matched known Laroux macro patterns. Laroux is a well-known Excel macro virus family that propagates by copying macro code into other Excel workbooks (often via global/template-style macro behavior), which can lead to widespread document contamination inside an environment even when there is no obvious “payload” like ransomware. The key risk here is not that Excel itself is malicious, but that opening a macro-infected workbook can enable macro-based replication and persistence across other spreadsheets, especially if macros are enabled or if the document is saved/used as a template source.

As a result, it’s likely this workbook should be treated as infected/suspicious and handled as a containment-and-cleanup scenario rather than a one-off benign macro. Depending on your policy and user actions, the macro may or may not have executed (for example, if macros were disabled, execution may not have occurred even though the macro was present). Recommended next steps typically include: isolating/quarantining the specific attachment and any copies of it, identifying other workbooks the user recently opened/modified that could have been contaminated, and removing the Laroux macro from affected documents using an approved cleanup approach (CrowdStrike provides guidance and a cleanup tool here: https://supportportal.crowdstrike.com/s/article/Release-Notes-Laroux-Malware-Cleanup-Tool). You may also want to review Office macro settings and audit for additional Excel files with similar macro indicators to ensure the issue hasn’t spread.

CustomFields.investigationanalysis:
Analysis:

Alert triggered for CTM-Password Spraying Activity Detected in SQL Server.

Log Source Time: Aug 15, 2026, 3:06:43 PM

Event Name: LOGIN - LOGIN FAILED
 Low Level Category: Database Login Failed

Source IP observed: 10.61.56.138 towards same Destination IP 10.61.56.138.
 SQL Server Instance observed: INMUPA0119WD10.

Checked alert details and observed multiple SQL login failure events within a short duration.

The usernames observed in the provided events include entldbreader and sa.

In the payload, the following failure message was observed:

"Login failed for user 'entldbreader'. Reason: Could not find a login matching the name provided."

Client IP: 172.17.249.64
 Host Name: cdctsocva
 Application Name: Microsoft JDBC Driver for SQL Server

Multiple SQL login failures within a short period matched the correlation rule threshold and triggered the offense CTM-Password Spraying Activity Detected in SQL Server.

The failed login attempts originated from client IP 172.17.249.64 / host cdctsocva and were directed toward SQL Server INMUPA0119WD10.

The payload confirms that the login attempt for entldbreader failed because SQL Server could not find a matching login for the provided username.

The provided events also show failed login attempts involving the sa account. All observed events are categorized as Database Login Failed, and no successful SQL authentication associated with these attempts was observed in the provided alert details.

The alert was triggered because multiple failed SQL login attempts were observed within a short period, including attempts against different SQL usernames such as entldbreader and sa, which matched the password spraying correlation rule threshold.

As checked with the respective team, they confirmed that the observed login failures are expected and occurred because these usernames are not configured/present in the SQL Server.

No successful authentication associated with the failed SQL login attempts was observed in the alert details.

Nothing suspicious observed from the available alert details.

Hence, closing this case as false positive.

As checked sender ID seen as theteam@truepennyadvisers.com
no recepient details observed
subject line : Vivo Wellness Webinar series - Wednesday 16 September 2026 - Eat for Life: The Longevity Diet Revolution

links observed are clean 
1 pdf attachment observed and sandboxing  result is clean
The PDF was manually validated and contains a webinar invitation poster for the "Vivo Wellness Webinar" titled "Eat for Life: The Longevity Diet Revolution" scheduled on 16 September 2026.

The email is a wellness webinar invitation promoting a nutrition and longevity session hosted as part of the Vivo Wellness Webinar series. The email content, Zoom registration links, sender information, and attached webinar flyer are aligned and consistent with the advertised event. No phishing, credential harvesting, impersonation, or malware indicators were identified.

Verdict : Advertisement/marketing
Action required : No action required.
Hence closing this case as False Positive.

Since all login attempts were unsuccessful and no signs of compromise were identified, nothing suspicious was observed beyond the failed authentication attempts.
Hence, closing this case as FP.

CustomFields.investigationanalysis:
Analysis:
Alert triggered for CTM-High frequency of privileged service calls DPAPI abuse (Event Id 4693).

Observed source and destination IPs 172.30.1.50(INKOLGPRDC4) which is internal Domain Controller servers within the TCS environment.

Event name observed as "Success Audit: Recovery of data protection master key was attempted" with Event ID 4693. Username associated with the activity is da.2287796.

The event indicates that a DPAPI (Data Protection API) Master Key Recovery operation was attempted. DPAPI is a native Windows security feature used to protect sensitive information such as saved credentials, certificates, browser passwords, and application secrets.

Investigation identified multiple successful Event ID 4693 logs from domain controllers INKOLGPRDC4.India.TCS.com. The activity was generated from the user account da.2287796, which is a privileged domain administration account.

The observed events are Success Audit events only. No corresponding failure events, unauthorized access attempts, suspicious authentication activity, malware execution, privilege escalation, lateral movement, or other indicators of compromise were identified.

The activity originated and terminated on the same domain controller systems (local-to-local communication), which is consistent with legitimate administrative or system-level operations involving access to DPAPI-protected data.

Team confirmed that the account da.2287796 belongs to the Wintel ADS Team, and the affected systems are managed Domain Controllers routinely accessed for administration, monitoring, service validation, and maintenance activities.

Based on the observed successful audit events, internal domain controller activity, administrative account usage, and team validation, the activity appears to be legitimate administrative behavior rather than DPAPI abuse.

Hence closing this offense as False Positive.

CustomFields.investigationanalysis:
Analysis:
Alert triggered for CTM- Excessive Blocked Traffic from Single IP.
The alert involves source IP 34.62.57.225 (Google LLC / Google Cloud Infrastructure) targeting destination IP 10.40.50.221.
Additionally checked the IP reputation and observed that 4/89 security vendors flagged this IP address as malicious on VirusTotal.
AbuseIPDB shows this IP address has been reported 38 times with a Confidence of Abuse score of 100%.

Further review of the offense details identified 29 events categorized as Potential Web Exploit and Access Denied. 
The events were generated from F5 ASM logs and correlated through the CRE rule "CTM- Excessive Blocked Traffic from Single IP".

Additionally reviewed the offense annotations and observed that multiple suspicious web application requests were detected and blocked by the F5 ASM Web Application Firewall. 
The source generated repeated requests within a short duration, indicative of automated reconnaissance or exploitation activity targeting publicly exposed web application resources.

Observed that the actual action was blocked.
The source IP belongs to Google Cloud Infrastructure (Google LLC) and is hosted within a cloud environment. 
The IP has a poor reputation based on external threat intelligence sources and has been reported for abusive activity by multiple security vendors and community feeds.

Further analysis indicates that the suspicious activity was related to web application probing and exploitation attempts. 
The offense was generated under the Potential Web Exploit category, and all associated requests were denied by the F5 ASM security controls before reaching the protected application.

No evidence was observed of:
 Successful exploitation
 Unauthorized access
 Privilege escalation
 Malware execution
 Persistence mechanisms
 Command execution
 Data theft or exfiltration
 Impact to the destination host
All malicious or suspicious requests associated with this offense were successfully blocked by the F5 ASM WAF, preventing any compromise of the destination asset.

Although the source IP has a malicious reputation and abuse history, it belongs to Google Cloud Infrastructure. 
Blocking the entire IP may affect legitimate cloud-hosted services utilizing the same infrastructure.

Hence, the IP is recommended to remain under monitoring, and blocking may be considered only if further malicious activity is observed or business validation confirms no legitimate dependency.

Conclusion:
The source IP 34.62.57.225 was observed performing suspicious web application reconnaissance/exploitation activity against destination IP 10.40.50.221. 
The activity triggered the CTM- Excessive Blocked Traffic from Single IP rule. 
All requests were successfully blocked by the F5 ASM WAF and no evidence of successful compromise or impact was identified.
Therefore, marking this alert as True Positive with No Impact.

CustomFields.investigationanalysis:
Analysis
Alert Analysis: Cisco ISE Failed Authentication Attempt
Alert Name: FAILED_ATTEMPT

Source Ip 10.249.147.10 and destination Ip is 10.249.250.246 both indicate internal communication
 Category: General Authentication Failed
Username	84-A9-38-66-68-26
 Severity: Medium (Severity 3)
 Source System: Cisco Identity Services Engine (ISE)
 Protocol: RADIUS

The authentication request originated from switch port GigabitEthernet1/0/11 on network device TCS-KOL-INFOSPACE-CITI-6H1-ASW1.
A Cisco access switch (TCS-KOL-INFOSPACE-CITI-6H1-ASW1) attempted to authenticate an endpoint with MAC address 84-A9-38-66-68-26 via MAC Authentication Bypass (MAB). The RADIUS authentication request was forwarded to the Cisco ISE server (10.249.250.246), which rejected the authentication attempt, generating a FAILED_ATTEMPT event.
Cisco ISE was unable to validate or authorize the endpoint and consequently denied access.
No other suspicious events observed in the logs.
Hence closing as false positive.

Analysis: CTM - Domain Admin Account Successful Login to Non-DC Server
Alert triggered for successful login of Domain Admin account "da.2887317" on host AZRHKSHAACN02, which is identified as a non-domain controller server.
The authentication event corresponds to Windows Event ID 4624 (Successful Logon) with Logon Type 2 (Interactive Logon), indicating a local console or direct user session login.
The logon was initiated through LogonUI.exe, a legitimate Windows component responsible for interactive user logins and session creation.
The account belongs to the CNMROOT domain and was granted an Elevated Token: Yes, confirming administrative privileges were assigned to the session.
Authentication Package: Negotiate and Logon Process: Advapi are standard Windows authentication mechanisms and do not indicate suspicious activity by themselves.
No Source Network Address or Source Port was recorded, suggesting this was not a remote network logon but rather a local/interactive authentication.
The login originated from the same host AZRHKSHAACN02, and no evidence of lateral movement or external source connections was observed from the provided event details.

Since this alert involves a Domain Admin account logging into a non-DC server, validation with the asset owner or administrator is required to confirm whether the activity was part of authorized administrative operations.

The alert was triggered due to a successful interactive login (Logon Type 2) by the privileged Domain Admin account da.2887317 on non-DC server AZRHKSHAACN02. Review of the event indicates the login occurred through the legitimate Windows process LogonUI.exe, using standard authentication mechanisms, with no suspicious source IP, network activity, or malicious indicators observed. Based on the available evidence, the activity appears consistent with authorized administrative access.

User validation was performed and the account owner confirmed that the 
authentication activity was authorized and related to legitimate administrative activity on AZRHKSHAACN02$.
No suspicious activity was observed.

Hence closing this case as False Positive.

Hi Kuldeep,

If the KING co-branding association is not fitting the current campaign direction, we can look at another strong media direction.

Tata Group can explore transit branding across airlines to build visibility across daily movement routes and commuter touchpoints.

We work across 150+ trains, including Vande Bharat, Tejas, Rajdhani and Shatabdi, along with 15+ global airlines, 1,00,000+ autos, cabs, buses, road shows and much more.

Would it be worth a quick 10-minute discussion to explore what fits Tata Group best?

Krutika Sharma
Excellent Publicity
+91 98989 46420 | inquiry@excellentpublicity.com
Member of BNI, Corporate Connections & Offline


On Sat, Sep 12, 2026 at 10:21 AM UTC Krutika Sharma <krutika@cricketadvertising.com> wrote:
Hi Kuldeep,

There is a high-impact co-branding association around SRK's KING that could work well for Tata Group.

The association includes bytes from Shah Rukh Khan, giving Tata Group a high-recall route to build visibility.

Can we schedule a quick 10-minute meeting to take you through how this can work for Tata Group?

Krutika Sharma
Excellent Publicity

Would it be worth a quick 10-minute discussion to explore what fits Tata Group best?

Username - C0-18-50-69-AF-48

As checked alert is triggered when at least 200 events are seen with the same Username in 1 minute.

Hence closing as False Positive.

This IP was reported 29 times. Confidence of Abuse is 100%: on AbuseIPDB.
IP is Present in Trusted IOCs in SOAR.

As checked logs over log source F5ASM @ TCS-UX-LB.tcs.com observed,

Event Name: Directory Traversal attempt "../" (Parameter)
 ActualAction (custom): blocked

HostURL (custom): businessreview.ultimatix.net

WAF_CommandDetails (custom): /api/file?path=../../.env

The request /api/file?path=../../.env is a directory traversal attempt where the attacker tries to manipulate the file path parameter to escape the intended application directory and access the sensitive .env file. Environment files often contain database credentials, API keys, tokens, and application configuration details. The use of ../../ indicates an attempt to move up the directory structure and retrieve restricted files from the underlying server.

requestMethod (custom): GET

user_agent (custom): Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; Bytespider; +https://zhanzhang.toutiao.com/)

This user agent is identified as ByteSpider, a web crawler associated with ByteDance services. However, threat actors can spoof user-agent strings, therefore the request should be evaluated based on its malicious payload rather than the user-agent alone.

As observed in the event, the source attempted to access the sensitive .env file through path traversal techniques, which is a common reconnaissance activity performed to identify exposed application secrets and server configuration details. The F5 ASM policy detected the malicious pattern and blocked the request successfully.

Actual action is Blocked for the observed suspicious request.

Keeping it under monitoring.

Closing it as TP with no impact.

CustomFields.triageexplanation:
The activity involved Microsoft Excel (`EXCEL.EXE`) being launched to open a workbook directly from a network share (`\\10.182.130.53\Special Finance\RBI\ADESH\FIRC\Allocation\26-27\pending repat sheet 01 jun 2026 onwards.xlsx`). While the detection record doesn’t include a human-readable description, the underlying telemetry indicates the workbook contained an embedded Excel macro whose identifiers and display characteristics align with the well-known “Laroux” macro family (a classic Excel macro virus pattern). In other words, the notable behavior here isn’t Excel opening a file from a share by itself—it’s that the document content appears to include a Laroux-style macro.

This was triaged as a true positive because Laroux is a recognized macro-based threat pattern: it typically propagates by copying macro code into other Excel workbooks and can spread quickly through shared drives and commonly used templates. Even when it doesn’t immediately show overtly destructive behavior, its presence is still meaningful because it indicates the document is not “clean” and may act as a propagation mechanism across users who open or save spreadsheets in the same environment. The network-share location also increases the potential blast radius, since shared finance folders are frequently accessed and can facilitate rapid spread if macros are enabled.

As a result, this detection should be treated as a confirmed identification of a Laroux-associated macro within the referenced workbook, and it may warrant containment and cleanup actions. Depending on your policy and how the endpoint was configured at the time, the sensor may have only generated an alert (without blocking), or additional prevention actions might have occurred—but that isn’t guaranteed from the “standard detection” disposition alone. Practically, you should assume the file could be a source of macro propagation and consider: isolating/quarantining the spreadsheet on the share, checking for other spreadsheets with similar macros in the same directory tree, and removing the macro content from affected documents (CrowdStrike provides a Laroux cleanup tool referenced here: https://supportportal.crowdstrike.com/s/article/Release-Notes-Laroux-Malware-Cleanup-Tool). Additionally, validate whether macros were enabled for the user/session and review nearby activity for other Excel files being modified or newly created around the same time, which can indicate attempted spread.

CustomFields.investigationanalysis:
Alert triggered -Multiple blocked hits on Akamai WAF followed by one success hit

The offense was generated because the same external IP (34.68.34.73) generated multiple blocked requests against TCS web assets and subsequently accessed a web resource that was configured in monitor/alert mode.

Review of the correlated events identified that the source IP initially attempted to access the path /.svn on www.tcs.com. Such requests are commonly associated with automated reconnaissance or vulnerability scanning activity, where attackers or internet scanners attempt to identify exposed Subversion (SVN) repositories.

The request was detected by Akamai WAF under rule BOT-BROWSER-IMPERSONATOR, classified as "Unknown Bots (Browser Impersonator)", and was successfully blocked with HTTP 403 (Denied), preventing access to the requested resource.

Subsequent events show the same source IP accessing a publicly accessible JavaScript resource hosted on www.ar.tcs.com. This request triggered Akamai reputation rule REP_4965860 - Web Attackers (Low Threat) due to the IP reputation score (WEBATCK=10, SCANTL=10). Since the rule was configured in monitor/alert mode rather than blocking mode, the request received an HTTP 200 response.

Analysis confirmed that the requested object was a standard static website component and not a sensitive application endpoint, administrative interface, or restricted resource. Review of the successful request determined that it involved only the retrieval of publicly accessible content and did not represent successful exploitation or unauthorized access.

Threat intelligence checks conducted against source IP 35.196.33.217 revealed the following:

VirusTotal: 3/89 security vendors flagged the IP as malicious.
AbuseIPDB: 937 reports with an Abuse Confidence Score of 71%.
User-Agent (custom): Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/100.0.4896.88 Safari/537.36

This user agent corresponds to the Google Chrome browser running on a Linux x86_64 system and rendering content using the Blink engine.

Additional review did not identify any evidence of successful web application exploitation, remote code execution (RCE), SQL injection, command injection, authentication bypass, unauthorized access to sensitive resources, webshell deployment, malicious file uploads, privilege escalation, lateral movement, internal reconnaissance, data access or exfiltration, impact to the destination server, or any follow-on malicious activity associated with the source IP during the investigation period.

The observed activity is consistent with automated internet reconnaissance and scanning originating from an external cloud-hosted IP address. Akamai WAF controls functioned as expected by blocking the suspicious reconnaissance request, while the subsequent allowed request was limited to the retrieval of a publicly accessible static resource. No indicators of compromise or evidence of successful attack execution were identified during the investigation.

Further keeping this IP under monitoring.

Hence, this case is assessed as a True Positive with No Impact.

Alert triggered for Reported  ANTISPAM/Phishing Email - Email Investigation
As checked sender ID seen as "MadMuscles <support@madmuscles.com>"
Recipient seen "kiran.mundiath@tcs.com"

x-sender= "support@madmuscles.com"
Mail sub line:YOU ARE WANTED 👀
As checked sender domain reputation(VT: Clean;Bright cloud: Clean; Url void: Clean;  Symantec: Clean; Urlscan: Clean)
As checked links in mail body -(VT: Clean;Bright cloud:Clean; Url void: Clean;  Symantec: Clean)

Mail about:
Summary: The email is a personalized fitness and weight-loss promotion from MadMuscles. The message uses the recipient’s name, age, weight, and goal, and encourages the recipient to reveal and start a customized workout plan through embedded buttons.
Verdict: The email appears to be legitimate marketing rather than spam, especially if the recipient previously registered with MadMuscles. However, because the message contains personal health-related details and external links, verify the sender and URLs before clicking or entering payment information.

No attachment found in the mail body  and  urls found redirecting to body morphing point and not taking any random credentials and nothing malicious found in the sandboxing.
And the content in the mail is not related to phishing.  
The mail which is related to   SPAM.
 
Verdict :  SPAM.
Action required : No action required
Hence closing this case as False Positive.

CustomFields.triageexplanation:
The activity involved Microsoft Excel (`EXCEL.EXE`) being launched to open a spreadsheet (`UISCE.xlsx`) directly from the user’s Outlook/Internet cache location: `C:\Users\170326\AppData\Local\Microsoft\Windows\INetCache\Content.Outlook\...\UISCE.xlsx`. That path is commonly used when a document is opened from an email attachment or a message preview. Falcon’s cloud-based machine learning then evaluated the contents/behavior associated with that document open event and identified macro-related indicators consistent with the Laroux macro family.

This was triaged as a true positive because the signals associated with the spreadsheet’s macros matched known Laroux macro characteristics (for example, macro naming/identifiers that are strongly associated with Laroux). Laroux is a well-known Excel macro virus family that typically propagates by embedding itself into Excel workbooks and can spread when infected documents are opened and saved. Even when it doesn’t immediately drop additional payloads, it’s still important because it can persist in documents, replicate across files, and create ongoing exposure through document sharing.

As a result, this detection suggests the workbook opened from the Outlook cache may contain Laroux-related macros, and the host/user may have been exposed to a macro-based infection vector. Depending on your policy settings and what occurred on the endpoint, Falcon may have only generated the alert (a “standard detection”) without automatically blocking Excel, and the macro may or may not have executed (execution often depends on whether macros were enabled and on Office security settings). Recommended next steps typically include: isolating and reviewing the specific `UISCE.xlsx` file, checking whether macros were enabled at the time it was opened, identifying any other recently accessed/saved Excel files that could have been infected, and cleaning/removing the Laroux macro from affected documents if confirmed (CrowdStrike provides a Laroux cleanup tool referenced here: https://supportportal.crowdstrike.com/s/article/Release-Notes-Laroux-Malware-Cleanup-Tool).

The activity involved Microsoft Excel (`EXCEL.EXE`) being launched to open a spreadsheet (`UISCE.xlsx`) directly from the user’s Outlook/Internet cache location: `C:\Users\170326\AppData\Local\Microsoft\Windows\INetCache\Content.Outlook\...\UISCE.xlsx`. That path is commonly used when a document is opened from an email attachment or a message preview. Falcon’s cloud-based machine learning then evaluated the contents/behavior associated with that document open event and identified macro-related indicators consistent with the Laroux macro family.

This was triaged as a true positive because the signals associated with the spreadsheet’s macros matched known Laroux macro characteristics (for example, macro naming/identifiers that are strongly associated with Laroux). Laroux is a well-known Excel macro virus family that typically propagates by embedding itself into Excel workbooks and can spread when infected documents are opened and saved. Even when it doesn’t immediately drop additional payloads, it’s still important because it can persist in documents, replicate across files, and create ongoing exposure through document sharing.

As a result, this detection suggests the workbook opened from the Outlook cache may contain Laroux-related macros, and the host/user may have been exposed to a macro-based infection vector. Depending on your policy settings and what occurred on the endpoint, Falcon may have only generated the alert (a “standard detection”) without automatically blocking Excel, and the macro may or may not have executed (execution often depends on whether macros were enabled and on Office security settings). Recommended next steps typically include: isolating and reviewing the specific `UISCE.xlsx` file, checking whether macros were enabled at the time it was opened, identifying any other recently accessed/saved Excel files that could have been infected, and cleaning/removing the Laroux macro from affected documents if confirmed (CrowdStrike provides a Laroux cleanup tool referenced here: https://supportportal.crowdstrike.com/s/article/Release-Notes-Laroux-Malware-Cleanup-Tool).

Even when it doesn’t immediately exhibit overt “malicious” behavior like ransomware, it is still important to treat it as a confirmed macro-based infection indicator and prevent further propagation.

Recommended next steps typically include isolating the affected host if you suspect spread, identifying and removing/cleaning the macro from the document(s), and checking for other spreadsheets that may have been infected by the same macro. triageexplanation:
The activity on the endpoint involved Microsoft Excel (`EXCEL.EXE`) being launched to open a workbook from the user’s Downloads folder: `C:\Users\3288776\Downloads\Procurement_Tracker_Departments.xlsx`. Falcon generated a cloud-based machine-learning detection tied to this Excel execution. Although the detection record doesn’t include a human-readable description, the telemetry associated with the document indicates the presence of a specific Excel macro signature (macro metadata such as display name/IOC value) consistent with the Laroux macro family.

This was triaged as a true positive because the workbook’s embedded macro characteristics align with known Laroux macro identifiers. Laroux is a well-known Excel macro virus family that propagates by copying macro code into other spreadsheets (often via global templates/startup behavior), which can lead to wider document-to-document spread inside an environment. Even when it doesn’t immediately exhibit overt “malicious” behavior like ransomware, it is still important to treat it as a confirmed macro-based infection indicator and prevent further propagation.

As a result, this detection should be treated as a confirmed presence of Laroux-style macro content in the opened spreadsheet, and it may warrant containment and cleanup actions. Depending on your Falcon prevention policy and how the process behaved at runtime, the sensor may have only alerted (without blocking) and allowed Excel to continue, or it may have taken some preventative action—this record alone doesn’t guarantee which occurred. Recommended next steps typically include isolating the affected host if you suspect spread, identifying and removing/cleaning the macro from the document(s), and checking for other spreadsheets that may have been infected by the same macro. If you want to remove the macro from documents, CrowdStrike provides guidance here: https://supportportal.crowdstrike.com/s/article/Release-Notes-Laroux-Malware-Cleanup-Tool

The activity on this endpoint was associated with the Windows **System** process, and Falcon generated a machine-learning–based detection. In addition to the generic “System” process context shown in the alert, Charlotte AI correlated the detection with **macro-related indicators** present in the event telemetry—specifically macro metadata (such as macro display names and embedded values) that are characteristic of the **Laroux** Excel macro family. This type of detection commonly occurs when an Office document containing a known macro pattern is opened or scanned, and the macro content is identified even if the visible process context is limited (for example, when the macro execution chain isn’t fully captured in the simplified fields shown here).

Charlotte AI triaged this as a **true positive** because the macro indicators observed match known Laroux macro characteristics rather than a generic or ambiguous ML-only signal. Laroux is a well-known Excel macro virus family; it’s often categorized as a potentially unwanted or legacy macro threat that can propagate through documents and templates. Even when it doesn’t behave like modern ransomware or a remote-access trojan, it can still introduce risk by spreading within document ecosystems, modifying spreadsheets/templates, and creating persistent “re-infection” scenarios if infected documents remain in circulation.

As a result, this detection may warrant **document-focused remediation** rather than host reimaging: you may need to identify and remove or clean the affected Office documents/templates that contain the Laroux macro so it doesn’t continue to spread internally. Depending on your policy and sensor settings, Falcon might have only alerted (without blocking), or it might have taken some preventative action—but that isn’t guaranteed from the “standard detection” disposition alone. If you want to remove the macro from documents, CrowdStrike provides guidance and a cleanup approach here: https://supportportal.crowdstrike.com/s/article/Release-Notes-Laroux-Malware-Cleanup-Tool.

CustomFields.triageexplanation: This detection was labeled **inconclusive** because the observed process chain and command-line arguments are strongly consistent with **legitimate Microsoft OneDrive update/maintenance activity**, but the same pattern can also be **abused for defense evasion or masquerading**. Here, `OneDrive.exe` is launched with `/updateInstalled /background` from `OneDriveSetup.exe` under `C:\Program Files\Microsoft OneDrive\Update\...`, and the parent/grandparent command lines include typical OneDrive updater switches such as `/allusers`, `/permachine`, `/childprocess`, `/renameReplaceOneDriveExe`, `/removeNonCurrentVersions`, and `/installWebView2`—all of which commonly appear during normal OneDrive servicing and component replacement. However, attackers sometimes leverage trusted, signed binaries (“living off the land”) or drop lookalike executables into expected paths to blend in, and command-line–based detections can’t always prove whether this was a routine update versus a staged execution path. Without additional corroboration (e.g., file signature validation, hash reputation, update timing/source, network destinations, or evidence of tampering/persistence), there isn’t enough to confidently call it benign or malicious, so it remains **inconclusive**.

CustomFields.triageexplanation: This detection was labeled **inconclusive** because the observed activity is a very common—and often legitimate—Office workflow, but it also overlaps with a well-known initial access pattern used in phishing. Here, **Explorer.exe** launched **Outlook.exe**, which then spawned **Excel.exe** to open an `.xlsx` file directly from Outlook’s **INetCache/Content.Outlook** location (the temporary cache where email attachments are stored). That chain strongly suggests a user opened an email attachment, which is normal in business environments; however, attackers frequently deliver malicious Excel documents the same way and rely on user interaction (opening the file, enabling editing/content, or triggering embedded content) to progress. Because the telemetry provided only shows the attachment being opened—without additional corroborating indicators such as macro execution, suspicious child processes (e.g., PowerShell/cmd/wscript), abnormal network beacons, or known-bad file reputation—the behavior cannot be confidently classified as benign or malicious based on this event alone, hence the **inconclusive** triage.

Unlimited Users to Conduct PAN India Audit using Mobile application

A suspicious binary alert was generated on host aks-nodepool-50592261-vmss0001KM belonging to cluster COIDWSPRDWEAKS001. The detection was triggered when /usr/bin/python3.12 created the file AstExtension under the Azure Monitor Agent extension path /var/lib/waagent/Microsoft.Azure.Monitor.AzureMonitorLinuxAgent-1.45.0/AstExtensionBin/. The process involved was /usr/bin/python3 -u /usr/sbin/waagent -run-exthandlers executed by the root user. The alert classified the binary as suspicious because it appeared packed or encrypted, a characteristic commonly associated with concealed executables.

The file path and execution chain indicates the activity originated from the Azure Linux Agent (waagent) while processing Azure VM extensions. The affected file is part of the Microsoft.Azure.Monitor.AzureMonitorLinuxAgent package used for Azure monitoring and telemetry collection. No additional indicators of compromise, unauthorized access, persistence mechanisms, or malicious process execution were observed during the investigation.

Further validation was performed with the AKS infrastructure team. The team confirmed that the activity was generated as part of an AKS node pool update/extension update and advised that the alert can be ignored as it is related to a legitimate platform update operation.
Hence, closing this case as FP.
